source_text: Sed nolo interim hunc morem veritati deputare. Consuetudo sit tantisper, ut consuetudini etiam consuetudinem opponam. Per Graeciam et quasdam barbarias eius plures ecclesiae virgines suas abscondunt. Est et sub hoc caelo institutum istud alicubi, ne qui gentilitati Graecanicae aut barbaricae consuetudinem illam adscribat. Sed eas ego ecclesias proposui quas et ipsi apostoli vel apostolici viri condiderunt, et puto ante quosdam. Habent igitur et illas eandem consuetudinis auctoritatem, tempora et antecessores opponunt magis quam posterae istae. Quid observabimus, quid deligemus? Non possumus respuere consuetudinem, quam damnare non possumus, utpote non extraneam, quia non extraneorum, cum quibus scilicet communicamus ius pacis et nomen fraternitatis. Una nobis et illis fides, unus deus, idem Christus, eadem spes, eadem lavacri sacramenta, semel dixerim, una ecclesia sumus. Ita nostrum est quodcunque nostrorum est. Ceterum dividis corpus. Tamen hic, sicut in omnibus varie institutis et dubiis et incertis fieri solet, adhibenda fuit examinatio, quae magis ex duabus tam diversis consuetudinibus disciplinae dei conveniret. Et utique ea deligenda quae virgines includit, soli deo notas, quibus, praeter quod a deo non ab hominbus captanda gloria est, etiam ipsum bonum suum erubescendum est. Virginem magis laudando quam vituperando confundas; quia delicti durior frons est, ab ipso et in ipso delicto impudentiam docta. Nam illam consuetudinem, quae virgines negat dum ostendit, nemo probasset, nisi aliqui tales quales virgines ipsae. Tales enim oculi volent virginem visam, quales habet virgo quae videri volet. Invicem se eadem oculorum genera desiderant. Eiusdem libidinis est videri et videre. Tam sancti viri est subfundi, si virginem viderit, quam sanctae virginis, si a viro visa sit.
thought_title: Custom on both sides, but the veiling custom is the one to choose
orientation: Tertullian is answering the claim that veiling virgins is only a local custom, by pointing to older churches founded by apostles that also veil virgins, and then arguing that the veiling custom is the one that befits God's discipline.
pass_a_gloss: But I do not wish for the present to count this custom as truth. Let it be custom for a while, so that I may oppose custom even to custom. Through Greece and certain barbarian regions of it, more churches hide their virgins. And under this sky also that institution exists somewhere, lest anyone ascribe that custom to Greek or barbarian gentility. But I have set before you those churches which the apostles themselves or apostolic men founded, and I think before certain ones. Therefore they also have the same authority of custom, times and predecessors they oppose rather than these later ones. What shall we observe, what shall we choose? We cannot reject a custom which we cannot condemn, as being not foreign, because not of foreigners, with whom of course we share the law of peace and the name of brotherhood. One faith is to us and to them, one God, the same Christ, the same hope, the same sacraments of the washing, I will have said once, we are one church. Thus ours is whatever is of our people. Otherwise you divide the body. Nevertheless here, as in all variously established and doubtful and uncertain matters is accustomed to happen, an examination had to be applied, which of two such different customs would befit the discipline of God more. And certainly that one is to be chosen which encloses virgins, known to God alone, for whom, besides that glory is to be sought from God not from men, even their own good is to be blushed at. You would confound a virgin more by praising than by blaming; because the front of a fault is harder, taught shamelessness from the fault itself and in the fault itself. For that custom which denies virgins while it displays them, no one would have approved, unless some such persons as the virgins themselves. For such eyes will want a virgin seen, as the virgin has who wishes to be seen. The same kinds of eyes desire each other mutually. It is of the same lust to be seen and to see. It is as much of a holy man to blush, if he has seen a virgin, as of a holy virgin, if she has been seen by a man.

lemmas.gloss: to blush at, be ashamed of

choices.why: The verb means to conceal from view; 'hide' keeps the physical sense of covering the virgins from sight, which is Tertullian's point.
Lavacrum is Tertullian's term for baptism; 'washing' preserves the literal image while 'sacraments' keeps the plural force.
The verb means to shut in or confine; 'encloses' conveys the protective seclusion Tertullian advocates.
The gerundive expresses obligation; 'is to be blushed at' keeps the passive obligation and the bodily image of blushing.
The potential subjunctive expresses a general truth; 'confound' captures the sense of shaming or discomfiting.
The deponent verb means to redden or blush; 'blush' keeps the physical sign of modesty Tertullian values.

pass_b_english: But for now I do not want to count this custom as truth. Let it remain custom for the time being, so that I may set custom against custom. Throughout Greece and certain barbarian parts of it, many churches hide their virgins. This practice exists somewhere under our own sky too, so that no one can ascribe that custom to Greek or barbarian gentile ways. But I have put forward those churches which the apostles themselves or apostolic men founded, and I think before certain others. They have the same authority of custom, and they plead their times and predecessors more than these later churches of ours do. What shall we observe? What shall we choose? We cannot reject a custom we cannot condemn, since it is not foreign, because it belongs not to foreigners, with whom we share the bond of peace and the name of brotherhood. We and they have one faith, one God, the same Christ, the same hope, the same sacraments of baptism. Let me say it once: we are one church. So whatever belongs to our people belongs to us. Otherwise you divide the body.

Yet here, as is usually done in all matters variously established and doubtful and uncertain, an examination should have been applied: which of two such different customs better befits the discipline of God. And certainly the one to be chosen is the one that encloses virgins, known to God alone. For them, besides the fact that glory is to be sought from God and not from human beings, even their own good is to be blushed at. You would confound a virgin more by praising her than by criticizing her, because the forehead of sin is harder, taught shamelessness by sin itself and in sin itself. For no one would have approved that custom which denies virgins while it displays them, except people just like the virgins themselves. For the kind of eyes that want a virgin to be seen are the kind a virgin has who wants to be seen. The same kinds of eyes desire each other. It belongs to the same lust to be seen and to see. It is as much the mark of a holy man to blush if he has seen a virgin as it is of a holy virgin if she has been seen by a man.

problems.quote: the face of sin is harder, having learned shamelessness from sin itself and in sin itself
problems.source_quote: quia delicti durior frons est, ab ipso et in ipso delicto impudentiam docta
problems.why: 'frons' here means 'forehead' (metaphor for brazenness), not 'face'; 'impudentiam' is 'shamelessness' but 'docta' means 'taught', not 'having learned'.
problems.fix: because the forehead of sin is harder, taught shamelessness by sin itself and in sin itself
problems.ruling: Latin 'frons' = forehead (metaphor for stubbornness), not generic 'face'; 'docta' = taught, not 'having learned'

edits.old: because the face of sin is harder, having learned shamelessness from sin itself and in sin itself
edits.new: because the forehead of sin is harder, taught shamelessness by sin itself and in sin itself

fixed: Corrected 'face' to 'forehead' and 'having learned' to 'taught' to match 'frons' and 'docta' in the source.

problems.quote: they set their times and predecessors against these later churches of ours
problems.source_quote: tempora et antecessores opponunt magis quam posterae istae
problems.why: The later churches are the weaker party in a comparison, not the thing opposed. The comparative force of magis is lost.
problems.fix: they plead times and predecessors more than these later churches of ours do
problems.ruling: 'magis quam posterae istae' is a comparison, with the later churches as the compared subject. The English makes them the object of 'opponunt' and drops 'magis quam', which is a grammatical misreading.

edits.old: they set their times and predecessors against these later churches of ours
edits.new: they plead their times and predecessors more than these later churches of ours do

fixed: Fixed magis comparison: 'tempora et antecessores opponunt magis quam posterae istae' with nominative 'posterae istae' means more/stronger plea, not opposition directed at later churches.
Left 'forehead of sin is harder, taught shamelessness by sin itself and in sin itself' alone: correct for 'delicti durior frons est, ab ipso et in ipso delicto impudentiam docta'.

polish.changed: Clarified 'sacraments of the washing' as 'sacraments of baptism'; broke up long sentences and added paragraph break where the thought turns; made pronoun references and speaker continuity clearer for modern readers.

notes.quote: the same sacraments of the washing
notes.why: 'Sacraments of the washing' is unclear; likely means baptism.

last_rejected.quote: even their own good is to be blushed at
last_rejected.source_quote: etiam ipsum bonum suum erubescendum est
last_rejected.why: Subject is the virgins themselves, not 'their good'; they must blush at themselves.
last_rejected.fix: even they themselves must blush at their own good
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'ipsum bonum suum erubescendum est' is impersonal; translation 'their own good is to be blushed at' matches source.

last_rejected.quote: because it belongs not to foreigners, with whom we share the bond of peace and the name of brotherhood
last_rejected.source_quote: quia non extraneorum, cum quibus scilicet communicamus ius pacis et nomen fraternitatis
last_rejected.why: The relative clause attaches to the churches who are not foreigners; English makes foreigners the ones who share peace and brotherhood.
last_rejected.fix: because it belongs to people who are not foreigners, with whom we share the bond of peace and the name of brotherhood.
last_rejected.ruling: English follows the Latin syntax: 'non extraneorum, cum quibus' has 'extraneorum' as antecedent. The sense, that these are not foreigners because we share peace with them, still comes through.
